lesson.title: Content Delivery Networks: Moving Content Closer to You
lesson.summary: A CDN is a globally distributed set of cache servers that store copies of content close to end users, so requests can be served quickly from a nearby edge location instead of a distant origin server.
lesson.body:
The application layer is where content actually gets requested and delivered, an HTTP request for a video file or a web page, for example, and internet topology determines the physical and logical path that request and its response have to travel. Put those two together and a problem becomes obvious: if the server holding that content sits in one specific data center region, and users requesting it are scattered across the entire globe, every single request has to cross a long, and often congested, path to reach that one origin, and every response has to travel just as far back.

A content delivery network addresses this by distributing copies of content across many geographically spread out cache servers, often called points of presence, or PoPs, positioned in cities and regions close to where users actually are. When a user requests content that is handled by a CDN, some combination of DNS based routing and anycast addressing directs that request to a nearby PoP rather than all the way to the original, origin, server. If that PoP already has the requested content cached, a cache hit, it serves it directly from nearby, without the request ever needing to reach the origin server at all. If it does not have it cached yet, a cache miss, the PoP fetches the content from the origin once, caches a copy, and serves it, so that subsequent requests for the same content from nearby users become cache hits.

Streaming video is a clear, concrete example. Suppose a video is originally hosted on a server in Virginia, and the first person to watch it is in Mumbai. Without a CDN, every bit of video data for that viewer would have to cross an ocean and traverse many networks each time, adding significant latency and risking buffering, and the origin server in Virginia would bear the full load of every viewer worldwide. With a CDN, that first Mumbai viewer's request likely causes the video to be cached at a PoP physically near Mumbai. Every subsequent viewer in that region gets the video served from that nearby cache, with dramatically lower latency and without adding any further load to the distant origin server.

CDNs are not limited to video or large media files, they are also commonly used to cache static website assets like images, stylesheets, and scripts, and increasingly to accelerate and protect API traffic as well. Cached content is typically served with an expiration policy, a time to live, after which the cache checks back with the origin to make sure it is not serving stale data. The core idea throughout is the same one this concept builds on: moving content physically closer to the point of demand shortens the path that data has to travel, and a shorter path, across the internet's real topology, generally means lower latency and less congestion.
